summary: A travel-essay style piece on how indigenous storytelling traditions treat ancestral spirits and totems as living wisdom. The author recounts 2023 encounters with storytellers and artisans among the Yanomami, Haida, Lakota, Zuni, Ticuna, Maori and Huli, each describing how stories, totems, carvings, weaving or drums carry ancestral memory. It concludes that stories are compasses linking past, present and future.
one_line: A first-person essay on indigenous storytellers across several cultures who describe ancestral spirits, totems and craft as living carriers of tradition.
key_facts: On September 5, 2023, the author met Marina Silva, a Yanomami storyteller from Brazil, who described the 'xapiripë', spirits visualized during shamanic ceremonies.
Marina Silva said "Every creature, plant, and person is touched by the spirits," and that stories honor the spirits so they keep the people alive.
In late September the author listened to Michael Redbear, a Haida elder, beside a campfire in the Pacific Northwest surrounded by totem poles.
Michael Redbear said each figure on the totems is a story of the ancestors and a reminder not to stray from their accumulated wisdom.
On October 20, 2023, Grace Black Elk, a Lakota fabric weaver, explained that the horse is a totem symbolizing freedom, mobility and a deep connection with the spirit world.
Grace Black Elk said the horse's spirit carries the people's prayers to the Great Spirit.
Andrea Chikyaytella, a Zuni artisan, said stone fetish carvings carry breath, will and spirit; the bear fetish guards health and the eagle bears prayers to the AboveWorld.
The Zuni celebrated their Pekwin on September 12, 2023, when the author visited them in the Southwest.
On November 3, 2023, Eduardo Campos, a Ticuna keeper of myths in the Amazon, used the tambor drum to set the pace of his stories and said it helps people navigate the river of time.
On December 10, 2023, the author met Amira Heke by the fireside of the Maori tribe; her tales featured heroes, monsters and ancestry.
On September 29, 2023, in the highlands of Papua New Guinea, Timothy Duna, a Huli sorcerer, spoke of the 'ambua', ancestral spirits whose favor is courted through storytelling.
The essay argues that totems are a living language that evolves, unlike dead scripts etched in stone, and that elders are 'human totems' who steward their people's stories.
